clue.text: Matrimonial missiles soft and colourful

parts.note: describes the little paper scraps thrown over a newly married couple, light, soft and brightly coloured

explanation.surface: Guests at a wedding pelt the couple with something harmless and bright.
explanation.walkthrough: An old-style descriptive clue: there is no wordplay, just a playful picture of wedding 'missiles' that hurt nobody.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiny coloured paper pieces are traditionally thrown over bride and groom as they leave the ceremony.

clue.text: Her make-up could be one of pride in race perhaps

indicators.note: make-up is a composition, so the letters are made up anew in a different order

parts.note: a pride is a group of big cats, so one of them is a lion
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman's make-up might reveal her racial pride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Her' is the whole definition: a pronoun standing for a woman, so a girl's name. A pride is a family group of big cats, and 'make-up' shuffles the combined letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A female first name, so it can stand for the woman referred to as her.

clue.text: Hours spent keeping Eve, and Aurora apart

definitions.text: Hours spent keeping Eve, and Aurora apart

parts.words: Hours spent keeping Eve, and Aurora apart
parts.note: Eve is evening and Aurora the goddess of dawn: the dark hours lie between dusk and daybreak

explanation.surface: Someone spends hours trying to keep two women, Eve and Aurora, away from each other.
explanation.walkthrough: Eve reads as a woman's name but means evening; Aurora, Roman goddess of the dawn, means daybreak.
explanation.definitionFit: The dark hours between evening and dawn.

clue.text: Heart-shaped space traveller?

indicators.note: shaped means the letters of heart are formed into a new shape

explanation.surface: A heart-shaped spacecraft or alien voyager.
explanation.walkthrough: The planet is a space traveller because it orbits the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Our planet journeys endlessly through space in its orbit around the sun.

clue.text: ell, it sounds, at the back

definitions.text: ell, it sounds, at the back

parts.words: ell, it sounds, at the back
parts.note: ell is the last part of the word hell, and dropping the aitch, as in a Cockney 'ell, leaves only that back portion sounded

explanation.surface: A Cockney exclamation heard from the back.
explanation.walkthrough: With the H dropped, 'ell is what is heard of hell: only its back portion is sounded.
explanation.definitionFit: The very last or back portion of something.

clue.text: "Lend the eye a terrible ___" (Hen V)

parts.note: a quotation from Henry V's speech before Harfleur, with its last word left blank for the solver to supply

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Henry V with its final word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: in 'Once more unto the breach' Henry urges his men to 'lend the eye a terrible aspect'.
explanation.definitionFit: The quoted line ends with the word for appearance or look, completing Henry's call to look fierce in battle.

clue.text: Hot-headed beauty in the garden

parts.note: a garden bloom whose big yellow head looks like the blazing sun and turns to follow it

explanation.surface: A fiery-tempered beauty is out in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot-headed' suggests a temper, but the flower's head resembles the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall garden plant with a large golden head resembling the sun.

clue.text: Bronco-buster aims to do so in tandem

definitions.meaning: a rodeo rider wants to finish the ride still on the horse's back
tandem means arranged one behind the other, the ends touching

explanation.surface: A rodeo rider aims to perform with a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: A bronco-buster tames wild horses; the first reading splits the answer as END ON, finishing still on the horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Finishing still mounted is the rider's aim, and things placed one behind another, like horses harnessed in a line, meet each other at their ends.

clue.text: Occupation for a number on the river

indicators.note: in a down clue on means placed above the next piece

parts.note: ten is a number
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A numbered house or job is offered beside a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ure is a Yorkshire river, common in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenure is the holding or occupying of a property or post.

clue.text: His horseplay may make us rash

definitions.text: His horseplay may make us rash

indicators.note: may make signals that the letters of us rash can be formed into another word

explanation.surface: A cavalry officer's rowdy pranks could make us reckless.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines a light cavalryman whose 'horseplay' is both pranks and riding.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier of a light cavalry regiment, so his work is done on horseback.

clue.text: First name your dance, Sir !

definitions.meaning: Sir ... de Coverley is an old English country dance, so the dance belongs to this Sir

explanation.surface: Someone invites a knight onto the floor, asking his first name and offering him a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Roger de Coverley is a traditional English country dance, often the last dance of the evening.
explanation.definitionFit: A common male given name, and the knight whose name titles the country dance Sir Roger de Coverley.

clue.text: Goad union to reform this fossilized old body

indicators.note: to reform is to shape anew, so the letters of goad union are put into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A political agitator is told to prod a trade union that has grown fossilized and out of date.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text carries a stray '15' that the printed page lacks. 'to reform' rearranges GOAD UNION; 'fossilized old body' reads as a hidebound union but means a dinosaur skeleton.
explanation.definitionFit: A large plant-eating dinosaur known from fossil remains, one of the first dinosaurs ever identified.

clue.text: In the minority, lacking one of these ?

definitions.text: In the minority, lacking one of these ?

parts.words: In the minority, lacking one of these
parts.note: minority here is legal youth, being under age; a young person traditionally got the key of the door only at twenty-one

explanation.surface: Someone outvoted and in the minority finds themselves without something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minority' suggests being outnumbered, but means being under age: by tradition you were given the key of the door at 21. The held text has a stray '17' the page lacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Front-door keys letting the holder come and go freely, a privilege of coming of age.

clue.text: Row to starboard in this vessel

parts.note: a row is a line, as of houses or chairs
starboard is the right-hand side of a ship, abbreviated R for right

explanation.surface: Sailors are told to row towards the starboard side in this boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like a rowing order but is a noun meaning line.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocean-going passenger ship of a shipping company is a kind of vessel.

clue.text: Heeding perhaps when Pegasus spoke

definitions.note: a clause describing what the winged horse did when it made a sound, a past-tense verb

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of heeding might be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: Someone paid attention when the mythical winged horse spoke.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse's cry is a whinny, so the winged horse Pegasus would make that sound when speaking.

clue.text: Whither Gray's ploughman, going south ?

parts.note: in Gray's Elegy the ploughman plods his weary way towards his house at dusk; going south refers to the entry being read downwards

explanation.surface: Asking where the ploughman of Thomas Gray's poem is heading, travelling south.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard opens with the ploughman plodding his weary way home; 'going south' points to a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Towards one's house, the direction the ploughman takes at the end of the day in Gray's poem.

clue.text: Roses conflict in colour getting a prize

indicators.note: in places the conflict inside the colour word

parts.note: red is a colour
the Wars of the Roses were the English civil war between York and Lancaster, so the conflict is a war

explanation.surface: Red and white roses clash in colour at a flower show, one of them winning a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wars of the Roses were fifteenth-century English civil wars between the houses of York (white rose) and Lancaster (red rose).
explanation.definitionFit: Something given in recognition of an achievement, like a prize or bounty.

clue.text: Outlaw Adair and the November poet

parts.note: Robin Adair is the title of an old Irish-Scottish song, so Adair's first name is Robin
Thomas Hood wrote the poem November, which begins No sun, no moon

explanation.surface: An outlaw named Adair keeps company with a poet who wrote about November.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Robin Adair' is a traditional song; Thomas Hood's 'November' lists everything missing from the month.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary English bandit of Sherwood Forest who robbed the rich to give to the poor.

clue.text: Unknown item in the beer ? Something planted ? Found under the carriage

indicators.note: in places the unknown inside the beer

parts.note: ale is beer
in algebra an unknown quantity is written X
a tree is something planted

explanation.surface: Someone finds an unknown object in their beer and something planted under a carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: X is the usual algebraic unknown.
explanation.definitionFit: The bar or shaft on which a carriage's wheels turn, mounted beneath its body.

clue.text: Revolutionary device makes visionary lose his head

indicators.note: losing his head means the visionary's first letter is removed

parts.note: a visionary is a dreamer, one full of grand ideas

explanation.surface: A revolutionary invention drives its idealistic creator to lose his head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' hints at politics, but the tool rotates to enlarge holes.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotating cutting tool used to widen or finish a bored hole, so it works by turning.

clue.text: Be upset when bird's about to give a snub

indicators.note: about means the bird is around the other letters

parts.note: the ruff is a wading bird

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the letters of be read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is upset when a bird turns up to snub them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' in a down clue turns the little word upside down, giving EB; 'about' wraps the bird round it. The ruff is a European wading bird.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebuff is to reject curtly, which is giving someone a snub.

clue.text: Alice upset it at the Tarts trial

definitions.text: Alice upset it at the Tarts trial

parts.words: Alice upset it at the Tarts trial
parts.note: in Alice in Wonderland, at the trial of the Knave who stole the tarts, Alice grows large and tips over the seating for the twelve jurors

explanation.surface: Alice causes an upset at a trial over some tarts.
explanation.walkthrough: In chapter 12 of Lewis Carroll's book, Alice jumps up and knocks over the jurors' enclosure, spilling the creatures in it.
explanation.definitionFit: The enclosure in a courtroom where the jurors sit, the very thing Alice tipped over in Wonderland.

clue.text: Poor Joe gets wealthy within the old city

indicators.note: within puts wealthy inside the shuffled name
poor suggests the name Joe is in bad shape and rearranged

parts.note: wealthy means rich

explanation.surface: A poor man named Joe gets rich in an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' scrambles the name to give JEO, and 'within' sets the synonym for wealthy between its second and third letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient city of the Jordan valley whose walls fell to Joshua's trumpets.

clue.text: Fragrant place for old wrongdoers

definitions.meaning: scented garden flowers grown for their sweet smell
the wooden frame in which offenders were once locked by the ankles for public punishment

explanation.surface: A sweet-smelling spot where wrongdoers were once punished.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition stands for the scented garden flower by its quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Clove-scented garden flowers, and the old wooden frame holding offenders by the feet.

clue.text: Might be worth the dicey attempt

indicators.note: might be suggests the letters of worth could become another word

explanation.surface: A risky attempt could still be worth it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dicey' means risky in the surface but literally points to a cast of the dice.
explanation.definitionFit: A cast of the dice, an attempt whose outcome is down to chance.

clue.text: A sovereign for a judge, on a point of law ?

definitions.meaning: a monarch who reigns over a country

definitions.text: a judge, on a point of law
definitions.meaning: a judge who rules on a point of law gives a ruling

explanation.surface: Asking whether a king may stand in for a judge on a legal question.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a playful one: a judge who rules is one who rules.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch governs a kingdom, and a judge giving rulings on points of law is one who rules.

clue.text: But no, such gay measure for Miss Marten

definitions.text: But no, such gay measure for Miss Marten

parts.words: But no, such gay measure for Miss Marten
parts.note: Maria Marten was murdered in the Red Barn in 1827, so a cheerful dance in a farm building would be no happy event for her

explanation.surface: A suggestion of a merry dance for a Miss Marten is turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: The Red Barn Murder of Maria Marten in Suffolk was a famous Victorian melodrama; 'gay measure' is an old phrase for a lively dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A lively country dance once held in a farm outbuilding, the very kind of building where Maria Marten died.

clue.text: Make submission to postpone

definitions.meaning: to give way to another's wishes or judgement
to put off to a later time

explanation.surface: A request to submit and delay matters.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield respectfully to someone's opinion, and to delay or put off till later.

clue.text: Producing heat out of mechanical orifices

indicators.note: out of signals that the letters are taken from within the words mechanical orifices

explanation.surface: A machine's openings give off heat.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts in the last three letters of 'mechanical' and ends just before the last two letters of 'orifices'.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to calories, the units of heat energy, hence generating warmth.

clue.text: A story of defeat

definitions.meaning: a story (storey) is a level of a building
to defeat is to knock down or overwhelm someone, as a boxer is knocked down

explanation.surface: Someone tells a tale of being beaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Story' is used in its American spelling of storey, a level of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A storey is a level of a building, and to knock someone flat or baffle them utterly is to beat them.

clue.text: Emphasize need for the odd rest on board

indicators.note: on, in the phrase on board, places the letters inside the ship

parts.note: board stands for a ship, abbreviated SS for steamship

indicators.note: odd says the letters of rest are in a strange order

explanation.surface: A sailor insists he needs the occasional rest while at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board' means aboard a ship, SS (steamship), and the shuffled letters TRES (from 'odd') go inside it. 'need for the' only links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay weight on a point or syllable, accenting it.

clue.text: Time for a prisoner to get his oats

definitions.meaning: British slang for a stretch of imprisonment
oats boiled in milk or water make the breakfast dish

explanation.surface: A prisoner's sentence comes with his breakfast oats.
explanation.walkthrough: Doing porridge is British slang for serving a prison sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a jail term, and the hot breakfast cereal made from oats.
